#3288. The Best Tech Gifts From Sony Cameras, Sennheiser, HP, and Blink

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

The holiday gifting season is upon us, and there’s a good chance tech products are dominating your loved ones’ wish lists. But there is a wide range of gifts — at a very wide range of price points — if you’re trying to set your giftee up with the latest and greatest gadgets.

If you’re looking for budget-friendly tech gifts, the home tech category is a great option. Popular home tech products are typically less expensive than gaming consoles, nice headphones, and other staples, but they can be equally as useful for many giftees. One good example is the home security camera lineup offered by Blink. The Amazon brand offers some best-selling security upgrades that start well below $50 and make great gifts for all homemakers.

Another option is office gear, such as a new printer from industry leaders like HP. This route is especially good for younger people, such as college students or recent grads looking to set up their dorm or first apartment.

If you’re looking for a more substantial gift, audio and visual tech gifts are typically your best bet. On the audio side, one of our favorites this year is Sennheiser. The German brand has been putting out some great headphones that both audiophiles and average users can appreciate. On the visual side, we’re loving Sony’s cameras for any photographers on your list — especially if they’re relatively new to the art.

For all tech gifts, Best Buy is a great first stop. The electronics retailer is running some great deals during the holiday season, especially if you sign up for the My Best Buy Membership. This membership offers exclusive pricing, rewards, and extended returns/exchanges, all for the very reasonable price of $29.99 a year.

Here are four great tech gifts to pick up at Best Buy, starting at $28:

These little security cameras from Blink punch way above their price point, offering crystal-clear 2K resolution, wide coverage, and an intuitive app experience. The cameras also have two-way audio with noise cancellation, letting you communicate with people in your home while you’re away. Best of all, the two-pack of Blink Mini security cameras is currently available at Best Buy for just $27.99.

A great tech gift under $100 is this HP DeskJet 2955 all-in-one printer. It’s compact and easy to fit in most workspaces, but can still produce high-quality prints, scans, and copies. You also get HP’s AI technology that helps correct layouts, avoid mistakes, and alter content.

Sennheiser is putting out some of the best headphones on the market right now, including these Momentum 5s. The brand’s flagship consumer noise-canceling cans are built around 42-millimeter dynamic drivers that help deliver warm, detailed sound, no matter what genre you’re enjoying. The battery will last up to 57 hours, and, unlike most headphones, it’s also user-replaceable for real longevity.

If you’re shopping for an aspiring photographer, Sony’s Alpha 6400 is a great way to set them up for success. It’s smaller and more approachable than a traditional DSLR but still delivers exceptional image quality thanks to a powerful 24.2-megapixel Exmor CMOS sensor. Plus, it shoots 4K video and has a tilting touchscreen for getting different angles and easy menu navigation.

#3287. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3285. Google’s new Android XR glasses work with iOS, Made for iPhone certified

Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. There are 30 unique designs in total, and the frames weigh 40-44 grams with a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera.

Google’s Glasses companion client for iOS handles compute, including HDR processing, and saves images and videos (up to 90 seconds) to Apple Photos. The Made for iPhone certification comes into play for Wi-Fi Aware connectivity that allows for fast media transfers.

Gemini commands that use the camera, like visual search or translation, don’t trigger the light because those photos or videos are not saved anywhere, including Gemini History. Before that media reaches the cloud, Google redacts faces from video feeds and filters out bystander voices. This processing is done by the companion app. Additionally, that media isn’t used to train AI models or target ads.

Other key specifications include four microphones and two open-ear speakers. Besides voice commands with the “Hey Gemini” hotword, there is a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes. A physical on/off switch lets you wear Intelligent Eyewear as regular glasses.

On iOS, Gemini can make calls, send 1:1 messages (including via iMessage), and receive notifications.

Battery life is rated at nine hours on a single charge, while there’s a charging case that stores seven charges. Features include turn-by-turn Google Maps directions and real-time translation. On the streaming front, there’s support for Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, and Audible.

Google’s Android XR glasses require an iPhone 13 Pro or newer.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three frame designs, starting at $395 for optical and sun styles. Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear is available in the US and South Korea from $449.

Pre-orders open today with retail availability on December 10.

#3284. Johnny Depp's 'Ebenezer' a Box Office Hit, Fan-Favorite Years After Court Drama

Johnny Depp's return to the big screen landed at No. 1 at the international and domestic box offices this weekend years after his court drama ... despite a wide divide between critics and regular moviegoers.

"Ebenezer" opened domestically to the tune of $19 million and earned an additional $23 million overseas ... according to Variety and Deadline. Not bad for a budget of $38 million!

While the movie has split critics down the middle -- with the film sporting a 54% Tomatometer -- audiences have raved over it.

Currently the comeback flick is verified hot on Rotten Tomatoes with an 89% Popcornmeter rating ... and an A- CinemaScore.

The divide between fan reaction and critical response comes amid a flurry of analytical pieces that have tied the movie to some sort of PR power play by Johnny.

Take the Wall Street Journal's feature that says the film is the perfect PR vehicle for the star, while in a separate review, the WSJ claims the film fails to find its tone and that Johnny is "ridiculously blustery and loud as Ebenezer, as if trying to get laughs."

In another review ... Vanity Fair drew parallels further between Ebenezer and Johnny, characterizing the movie as "Christmas-washing" his reputation.

Johnny's return to Hollywood comes after he levied a defamation lawsuit against ex-wife Amber Heard over her 2018 Washington Post op-ed, in which she described herself as a "public figure representing domestic abuse." He claimed the piece falsely implied he was the abuser.

While a jury awarded Johnny millions in damages after siding with him, Heard won one count in her countersuit.

All in all ... it seems that Scrooges aside, Johnny has done it all in one weekend, returning to screens all over the world in a triumphant way.

#3283. The Apple Watch's New 'Siri Recap' Feature Is Even Creepier Than I Expected

The “Siri Recap” feature that Apple announced in September is finally available in a developer beta, and I’ve spent the last 24 hours with the feature turned on. It’s even more unsettling than the “Live Rewind” feature that launched at the same time. It listens to all my conversations, and produces summaries that are both helpful and deeply creepy.

I have a button in the watch’s Control Center that can turn the recapping abilities off, but if I forget to do so, Siri listens to everything. I’ll get a recap of my entire evening, presented in roughly hour-long chunks, including things I would have completely forgotten I had even heard about.

The recaps somberly mention silly memes my kids were laughing about, and make major bullet points out of offhand remarks from brief conversations. If a conversation sticks to a single topic, I’ll often get a reasonably good summary of it, with specific facts and numbers highlighted; but just as often, Siri will get confused and mix up several topics or completely mishear a name or phrase.

Apple has four features that it considers part of “audio intelligence":

Music recognition, better known as Shazam. We’ve had a version of this on the Apple Watch for a long time now, although it has some improvements and now identifies music automatically.

Sound recognition, which can notify you about doorbells and babies crying. A version of this launched in 2020 as an accessibility feature.

Live Rewind, which gives you an on-wrist transcript of the last 15 seconds of detected speech.

Siri Recaps, which summarizes entire conversations for you to read on your phone.

Live Rewind had the flashiest demo from the Apple event: A server rattled off the day’s specials at a restaurant, and then the Apple Watch-wearing diner checked his watch to see a readout of exactly which dishes had just been mentioned. The utility is both obvious and kind of unnecessary: Why wouldn’t you just ask the server to repeat the list while they’re standing right there?

I haven’t found myself using Live Rewind, except out of curiosity about how the feature works. I discovered that it doesn’t pick up song lyrics very well, and also that by the time I think to check what was just said in a conversation, more than 15 seconds has passed since the part I was unsure about. I haven’t yet found a reason to use it for real.

But Siri Recaps? Those are both useful and unsettling. I enabled the feature, and decided to test it out later. But since it was on, it dutifully listened in as I picked up my son from school and gave him an update on an ailing family member’s health. We stopped by the library, and along the way we chatted about a variety of things: holiday travel plans, library policies, and the possibility of humans living in space in the future. Siri was listening to it all.

At least for now, the feature is only available in a developer beta, so sign up for that now if you want to try it. You'll need an Apple Watch Series 12 (or Ultra 4) and an iPhone 16 or better, excluding the 16e. (I have a 16 Pro, so I'm good.)

After you're updated to 27.3, go into the Watch app, tap Siri, and turn on Siri Recap. You can set a schedule for when it should listen (for example, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., if you want it on for the work day but off for the evening). You'll need to set a passcode on your watch, and you'll be guided through a step to upgrade your audio connection. The control center on the watch will have a button you can use to turn Siri recaps on and off at will. To read your recaps, go to the Siri app on your phone.

But still: I feel weird publishing the contents of these recaps, because they do contain things that people said to me in what they assumed was a private setting. I had the feature on when I attended a choir practice, and Siri recapped the brief chats I had with other choir members before and after practice. (Interestingly, it did not recap any of the quiet conversations I had with fellow sopranos while the tenors were rehearsing their part. I’m not sure if the watch was unable to hear us over the music, or if Siri is programmed not to listen when music is being played.)

Because speakers aren’t identified, it seems Siri doesn’t know what to do when there is a disagreement. A human note-taker would jot down that Person A made a point in favor of something, and person B made a point against. But when my son and I disagreed about how likely space colonization might be in the future, the recap didn’t reflect the separate positions that were put forth. It summarized the conversation as including “debating the feasibility and timeline of human space colonization and asteroid mining,” which isn’t exactly accurate, but close enough.

When it comes to the content of the discussion, the recap notes a bullet point of “skepticism regarding permanent space colonies within the next 100 years.” It didn’t include my reasons for being skeptical, and didn’t mention my son’s opposing viewpoint at all. If I were using this recap to jog my memory of the conversation, it wouldn’t be all that helpful.

Details are sometimes egregiously incorrect. After a discussion about a family member’s health, the recap had notes on the prognosis of “father.” The family member we discussed is not anybody’s father. Names in general seem to be a problem; I recommended a book to my son, and the recap includes notes about the content of the book, but not its title. The book’s author appears in the introduction to the recap (sort of a summary of a summary), but not in the content of the recap itself where the book is mentioned.

I should probably turn Siri recaps off. It seems wrong to let people chat with me without letting them know that their conversation is being ... well, not technically recorded, but basically recorded.

But it’s so tempting to leave it on so that I can review my day. Some of the details in the recaps are useful, like the dates that were discussed as options for a holiday party. The recaps will be deleted in about a week (unless I save them to the notes app), so if I want to remind myself of a conversation a few days ago, I should be able to scroll back through my recaps and find it.

I would be a fool to rely on the recaps, though. The most important points of a conversation are often left out; Siri doesn’t know what’s actually important, and there’s no way to guide it as to what to pay attention to. Specific details can be wrong, as I mentioned. There’s also no way to control when a “conversation” starts or stops, unless you are turning the recap feature on and off from the watch.

And there’s more: Not only are names usually omitted (wait, who did she say I should ask about that project?), the few identifiers that make it into the recap, like names of events, are often wrong. Subjects of discussion are often conflated in really unhelpful ways: My husband mentioned paying for certain course registrations for one of our children, and later I talked to that child about an unrelated exam. The recap got all of these things mixed up with each other and was wrong about pretty much every detail. About all the recap could usefully do is to remind me that something about AP U.S. History was discussed. Reading the recaps can be like reliving your day entirely in the passive voice.

#3282. Wu-Tang Clan, Billy Idol, Phil Collins Enter Rock Hall at All-Star Induction Ceremony

It was difficult to imagine who could possibly top Wu-Tang Clan’s performance at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction on Saturday night at Los Angeles’ Peacock Theater. Following a spirited introduction from Chris Rock, all living members of the Staten Island hip-hop group hit the stage to perform a medley of some of their biggest hits, including “C.R.E.A.M.” and “Wu-Tang Clan Ain’t Nuthing ta F’ Wit.” The audience was on its collective feet screaming “Wu-Tang! Wu-Tang!” repeatedly as the mighty crew wielded their lyrical swords.

But then came the Red Hot Chili Peppers, who were part of Rick Rubin’s induction. Cosplaying Rubin (who, after an incredibly theatrical induction speech by Neil Young, accepted his honor in shorts, sandals and rose-tinted sunglasses), Anthony Kiedis, John Frusciante, Flea and Chad Smith erupted into their Blood Sugar Sex Magik single “Give It Away” donning fake white beards. After a short technical issue with Flea’s instrument, the ever-limber bassist and Kiedis continued to somehow defy aging and rocked it like it was 1991.

The high octane performances kept coming at a dizzying pace. The speeches were long (sans Rubin) and the event as usual ran well over four hours. But as Wu-Tang Clan and Rubin joined fellow honorees Queen Latifah, New Order/Joy Division, MC Lyte, Billy Idol, Iron Maiden, Luther Vandross, Sade, Oasis, Phil Collins, Celia Cruz, Fela Kuti, Gram Parsons, Linda Creed, Arif Mardin and Jimmy Miller, the excitement of “what’s next” made time disappear.

Of course several inductees opted not to show up (Oasis, New Order’s Bernard Sumner, Gillian Gilbert and Stephen Morris, Sade and Iron Maiden) and some of them were being inducted posthumously, but the Rock Hall was still able to make the evening magical with surprise presenters and performances.

U2 opened the show with “Silencio,” the lead single from their latest album, Carnaval de Luz, and their 1984 hit “Pride (In the Name of Love).” Jack Black joined St. Vincent, Metallica’s Kirk Hammett and Robert Trujillo and Rage Against the Machine’s Brad Wilk for an Iron Maiden tribute. MC Lyte came out firing on all cylinders for a cover of DJ Jazzy Jeff and the Fresh Prince’s “Boom! Shake the Room” before she was joined by Queen Latifah for “U.N.I.T.Y.” and “Ladies First” featuring Megan Thee Stallion and Remy Ma. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Usher sailed through Luther Vandross’ hits “So Amazing,” “Here and Now” and “Never Too Much” and blossoming British chanteuse Sienna Spiro had the nearly impossible task of covering Sade’s “Smooth Operator.” With her raspy vocals and slow, sensuous execution, it worked, though there was a sense nobody would have wanted to trade places with her.

Blink-182’s Travis Barker inducted the ailing Phil Collins. He talked about the immense impact Collins had on him as an aspiring drummer, saying, “He wasn’t just an incredible drummer. He was also a singer-songwriter and one of the biggest solo artists in the world. Songs like ‘Sussudio,’ ‘Take Me Home,’ ‘Easy Lover’ and ‘Against All Odds’ was the soundtrack to my childhood. And then there’s ‘In The Air Tonight,’ his first solo single with arguably the most badass drum fill of all time. You don’t even have to be a drummer to know that fill. When that part comes on, everybody plays air drums.”

With a cane and the aid of an assistant, Collins made his way to the stage and was greeted by a standing ovation. The 75-year-old appeared more feeble than anticipated, making the moment even more emotional. “I’m really not as bad as it looks,” he quipped. “I’m much better.” Related Content Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony to Kick Off as Planned Amid FAA Grounding Flights Debacle Iron Maiden’s Nicko McBrain Recalls Spinal Tap Moments Touring for ‘Somewhere in Time’ John Mulaney Has Many Thoughts on the 2026 Rock Hall Inductees — And Picks Next Year’s Class 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame: 10 Burning Questions About Oasis, Sade, Phil Collins, and More

Collins then gave a tearful speech about his life and career, saying, “I grew up just wanting to play the drums. Everything else has been a really happy accident. I can’t believe, when I look back, how life has gone.” He also addressed the whisperings of an upcoming tour. While he didn’t confirm it would (or even could happen), he did end with, “You haven’t heard the last of me yet. I can promise you that.” Collins was unable to perform, but Cynthia Erivo did her best rendition of “In the Air Tonight” with Barker behind the kit.

Oprah Winfrey was on deck to induct Vandross. She spoke about her personal connection to the singer, saying, “Luther always gave me great counsel and taught me a lot about what it means to live well. Used to tell me, ‘Girl, use all your good dishes for yourself.’ One of my favorite songs that I heard for the first time as I was leaving my studio in Chicago, really late one night, someone on my team had handed me a new cassette tape, and I put it in for the drive home.”

“Yes, it was the eighties when cars had cassette tapes, and it was a brand-new Luther Vandross tape. And when his smash hit song ‘Power of Love’ came on, I was already almost at my front door. But I kept driving around the block, driving around the block, around the block to hear it over and over again. I love that song, still do.”

She compared listening to “Power of Love” as a “spiritual experience,” adding, “Luther Vandross was somebody who sang with such passion and soul; it could reach something deep inside that you didn’t even know was waiting to reach.”

It felt like déjà vu when Trent Reznor stepped up to the mic to induct Joy Division and New Order. Seven years ago, the Nine Inch Nails maestro welcomed the Cure into the esteemed Hall and admitted he’d been “ambivalent” about “certain award ceremonies.”

But there he was in his thick, black-rimmed glasses recounting the history of both bands. Moments later, Peter Hook stood alone at the podium without Sumner, Gilbert or Morris, making it painfully clear the band was unable to put their differences aside.

“Now I’m here and I realize how special it is,” Hook said. “It’s like being part of a family, which I’m delighted about. Now I’m on my own, but I’m not alone … it’s been a wild 50 years, and I’ve been happy, I’ve been mad and I’ve been heartbroken in equal measures. But I’m still fucking here.” Hook then picked up his bass and joined Deftones and Chvrches’ Lauren Mayberry for “Love Will Tear Us Apart” and “Bizarre Love Triangle” with the same fervor he’s harnessed for decades.

The Oasis segment, however, was a sore spot. Liam and Noel Gallagher already declined the invitation, so their absence was expected. But Stephen Wilson Jr., a country artist with no ties to British rock whatsoever, performing “Wonderwall” almost felt like a slight to Oasis. Wilson knew it, too. Backstage in the press room, he was reminded that the Gallagher brothers will likely see the performance and there was a chance they’d roast him for it. He said he had “thick skin” and would be “honored” if he were to become the target of a Gallagher brothers’ joke, but coupled with the awkward introduction by Better Call Saul actor Bob Odenkirk (who satirized the Gallagher brothers’ “cheeky” attitudes for the HBO comedy series Mr. Show in the 1990s), it seemed like Oasis’ absence was just too massive of a hole to fill.

That’s not to say the Rock Hall didn’t try: Billy Idol was ushered into the Hall by No Doubt’s Gwen Stefani and Tony Kanal. Stefani called Idol’s music a “time machine” and recalled listening to him in the early 1980s. Idol’s speech didn’t fail to entertain either as he sometimes struggled to read the teleprompter.

“Rock & roll says we can be heroes,” Idol said. “In my case I called myself Billy Idol so I could be my own hero.” He and longtime guitarist Steve Stevens proceeded to perform “Rebel Yell” and “Eyes Without a Face” as a duet with Stefani.

In the press room, Idol didn’t field any questions but posed for the cameras with his signature lip snarl and fist pumps, though Stevens spoke at length.

“Music is such a universal thing that I got the opportunity at some point to stay at Billy’s parents’ house and got to see his record collection, his adolescent William Broad record collection, and they were a lot of the same records that I grew up on,” Stevens said. “We’re roughly the same age, so it was David Bowie, T. Rex, Slade, Sweet Reed. We grew up [differently], but the music and things that inspired us were very much the same.”

Stevens also talked about his hopes for future generations of rock stars, saying, “There’s not that many true rock stars around to replace a Billy Idol. Hopefully, we’ll inspire people, and there’ll be another Steve Stevens … I’ve seen them on YouTube playing the solo for ‘Rebel Yell’ and sometimes playing it better than I can, so hopefully that’s the next generation. From what I understand, a lot of the record companies are looking at, you know, ‘Wow, we really have to develop artists again,’ because just having the numbers of viewers on TikTok or something is not a career.”

The crescendo of the evening came as Public Enemy’s Chuck D, with his inimitable and commanding voice, introduced Aerosmith to the stage. Steven Tyler, Joe Perry and the rest of the band started playing the first few notes to “Walk This Way” before Tyler suddenly stopped and told Perry there was “something missing.” Just as they’d done at The Hollywood Bowl two weeks ago, Run and DMC appeared from opposite sides of the stage to perform the crossover smash, elating the crowd.

While the 2026 iteration of the annual ceremony was mostly a success, a few things were glossed over. Gram Parsons and Ed Sullivan’s segments felt incomplete. Rumors Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr were somehow involved with the Sullivan induction ran rampant backstage, considering the Beatles’ rich history with The Ed Sullivan Show, it would have made sense. But alas, it came and went without much fanfare. Trending Stories ‘SNL’ Cold Open: Jensen Huang, Tech CEOs Get a Crash Course in Female Spies ‘SNL’ Weekend Update Roasts Trump Admin Over Grounded Flights, Jensen Huang Affairs Could ‘Rubber Soul’ Be the Best Beatles Album? (Yes) ‘SNL’: Watch Phoebe Bridgers Perform ‘Bobby,’ ‘Still Standing’

The In Memoriam portion paid tribute to a long list of musical figures we’ve lost, including Afrika Bambaataa, Rob Base, producer Bob Power, Traffic’s Dave Mason, ZZ Top’s Frank Beard and the Grateful Dead’s Bob Weir, who deserved much more than a photo flashing across a screen. Dolly Parton, however, was allotted a significant highlight reel, capturing the magic that made Dolly Dolly.

But the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame exists to ensure they are remembered long after they are gone. It’s not perfect and maybe they don’t always get it “right.” Gene Simmons may still be infuriated that hip-hop and R&B are welcome. Iron Maiden still might scoff at the idea as a whole. The Gallagher brothers might stick up their middle fingers. But still, it goes on — what’s more rock and roll than that?

#3279. Russell Brand Accuser Waives Anonymity, Alleging She Was Raped By Star At Age Of 16

One of Russell Brand‘s accusers has waived her legal right to anonymity after the Forgetting Sarah Marshall star was imprisoned for rape and sexual assault.

In an interview with The Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin (watch below), Mia Latter alleged that she was orally raped by Brand in 2006, when she was aged 16 and he was 30. She alleged that Brand referred to her as “the child” during their relationship, which she now considers to have been emotionally and sexually abusive.

Latter was one of the four women who spoke to The Times, Sunday Times, and Channel 4 in 2023. Their testimony inspired other women to make criminal complaints against Brand, ultimately leading to his conviction at London’s Southwark Crown Court earlier this month. Related Stories News Russell Brand Accused Of Sexual Misconduct By Six More Women After Rape Conviction News BBC Boss Challenged By Staff Over Culture Of "Reverence" Towards Powerful Stars

Brand has consistently denied wrongdoing. When Latter’s allegations were first published in 2023, Brand denied the claims and said it was part of a campaign by the “mainstream media” to silence him. Watch on Deadline

Latter, now 37, has gone public because she is campaigning for a change in UK law, calling for the introduction of a “staggered” age of consent, mirroring some U.S. states, including Florida. This would outlaw relationships between 16 year olds and adults, but would protect relationships between teenagers who are above the age of consent.

Latter, who was known as Alice in earlier reporting, first met Brand in central London when she was out shopping. Brand, who was hosting MTV shows at the time, approached her in the street and asked for her number.

They exchanged texts, met for a date, and ended up back at his apartment. Latter alleged that Brand attempted to give her oral sex, even though she was “squirming” in her seat. Latter alleged that Brand requested that she keep their three-month relationship secret, though her parents were “distraught” by their association. Brand encouraged Latter to skip school, sending cars to pick her up.

Towards the end of their relationship, Latter alleged that Brand orally raped her. “He ended up forcing me against the headboard [of the bed] and I couldn’t move, and he orally raped me — and I was choking and crying,” she told The Sunday Times.

“I was trying to push him off, so he knew that I didn’t want him to be doing that, and so then I ended up having to hit him in the stomach to get him off. I’ve never hit anyone [before] and … he said: ‘I just wanted to see your mascara run.’”

Brand discussed his relationship with Latter during an appearance on The Megyn Kelly Show in April. He admitted that his relationship with Latter had been “exploitative” and that he had “manipulated” consent. During the same interview, he described his behavior with women as “awful but lawful.”

Latter said: “If [consent is] manipulated, it’s not given. That’s not how that works. I think also [in] doing that interview, he was quite successful in distracting people … by saying, ‘It was immoral, it wasn’t illegal.’ Well, actually something illegal happened within that relationship.”

Latter was interviewed by the police in 2024, but said she was told by the Crown Prosecution Service that she would not be included in the trial, partly because of Brand’s appearance on Megyn Kelly’s show. “I was devastated by it,” she told The Sunday Times.

Latter also expressed dismay at the media organizations and people who stood by Brand. “At times, I felt angrier with these media organizations than I have with him, because he’s a monstrous person, but to be that spineless,” she said. “He couldn’t have done this for so long without these people enabling it, and disregarding the women who made complaints at the time.”

On Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison after being found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. The Sun newspaper reported on Sunday that Brand has been moved to Littlehey Prison, a jail for men who have been convicted of sexual offenses.

#3278. 10 Hacks Every Reddit User Should Know

If you're looking for discussions, recommendations, or advice online, it's hard to avoid Reddit. From mainstream sports to niche crafts, it does seem that there's some kind of Reddit community for everyone. (And if there's not one, you can make one yourself.) If you're using Reddit, here are 10 hacks you should know about to improve your experience on the site.

Reddit used to let everyone view your post and comment history, but in recent years, you can make your profile private. You can hide your posts, comments, and the subreddits you're a part of. If you want to do this, click your profile icon once you've logged in to Reddit, and go to Settings > Profile. Alternatively, you can follow the direct link to Reddit's profile settings page. Click the drop-down menu next to Content & Activity, and select Hide all. You should also turn off Online Status on the same page to stop people from seeing when you're using Reddit.

Old Reddit lets you use the site's classic design, and I prefer it to the more modern UI. Old Reddit looks dated, but it doesn't have infinite scrolling, distracting animations, and a bunch of features designed to increase the time you spend on the platform. It's no wonder that Reddit is making it harder to access this version of the site. As long as it's around, you should switch to Old Reddit for a cleaner reading experience. You can do that by going to Reddit Settings > Preferences and enabling Default to Old Reddit. You can also visit old.reddit.com, though you'll need to sign in for access

Many subreddits use custom themes that range from beautiful to borderline unusable. If you want a more consistent UI across the site, you should disable these custom subreddit styles. Go to Reddit Settings > Preferences and turn off Use community themes. If you're using Old Reddit, click the preferences button in the top-right corner, and under "display options," disable allow subreddits to show me custom themes.

A multireddit is a feed that shows posts from a customized group of subreddits. You can think of it as a way to break out of Reddit's algorithms, and create your own Reddit feed. I use multireddits to follow all sports-related subs I'm interested in. I even have one for gaming, and one for fountain pens. It's a great way to create interest-specific feeds, and if you make them private, no one else can see them. To create one, click the Create custom feed button in the left pane in new Reddit. In the Old Reddit design, click the Create button in the left pane. Be sure to select the Private button to keep it from showing up for others. You can add as many subreddits as you like to the list, and bookmark the feed to access it whenever you wish to.

Reddit has recently adopted an Instagram-like experience for its feeds. It removed the ability to sort posts by new, controversial, best, etc., and instead offers "For You" and "Following." If you dislike this change, you can bypass it. I use Reddit on mobile Safari, and I recommend an extension called Sink It for Reddit. It can automatically redirect you to Old Reddit, and there's a feature that optimizes it for mobile, which brings back the old sorting options. You can also use third-party apps such as RedReader for Android, or RDX for Reddit on an iPhone or iPad to restore the old sorting options for Reddit posts.

After all these years, Reddit's built-in search still leaves something to be desired—at least, on the surface. To find posts on Reddit faster, use search filters on the site. For instance, adding "title:" to your search will limit the results to post titles, and boolean operators such as AND, OR, and NOT also work for advanced searches on the site.

#3276. Robert Christgau and Carola Dibbell Talk New Documentary ‘The Last Critic’ and Staying Crazy in Love

The Last Critic is one of the year’s most fascinating rock documentaries — even though it’s not about a musician. It’s a portrait of the legendary writer Robert Christgau, the self-proclaimed “Dean of American Rock Critics.” He was one of the pioneers who invented pop-music criticism in the Sixties — but six decades later, at 83, he’s still at the top of the game. He began his Consumer Guide column in the Village Voice in 1969, and has kept cranking it out ever since, now on Substack. For generations of music fanatics, Christgau’s voice hits like Bob Dylan or Neil Young — two artists his age who are still doing it with the same fiercely independent spirit he brings to his writing.

The debut feature from director Matty Wishnow, The Last Critic won the jury prize at the South by Southwest and Oak Cliff Film festivals, as well as the 2026 Screen Dallas grand prize. It gets its New York premiere tomorrow. The film, which is co-produced by longtime Rolling Stone contributor and editor Joe Levy, goes beyond music, because it’s also the portrait of a marriage. Christgau and his wife, novelist Carola Dibbell, have been together more than 50 years. Over the decades, they’ve shared an intellectual life, raised their daughter, collected way too much vinyl, and — the weirdest part — remained crazy in love.

Christgau has a fearsome rep for never pulling his punches, with his own savage wit. Lou Reed spent a chunk of his live album Take No Prisoners complaining about getting a B+ grade for Street Hassle; when U2 won the Grammy Award for Album of the Year in 1988 for The Joshua Tree, Bono jokily groused in his speech about his band’s reviews in the Village Voice. Christgau’s inspired more songs attacking him than any other journalist, from Sonic Youth (“Kill Yr Idols”) to Public Enemy (“Bring the Noise”).

But there’s something obsessive about his lifelong quest to chronicle the music, still going strong after 60 years — he’s heard more albums than anyone on the planet. When he reviewed Prince’s Dirty Mind in 1980, he dropped one of the most-quoted one-liners in critical history: “Mick Jagger can fold up his penis and go home.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

The Last Critic features artists Christgau has reviewed, as well as writers he’s inspired, from Sonic Youth’s Thurston Moore to Pulitzer-winning novelist Colson Whitehead. (I make an appearance as well.) There’s a touching interlude with his lifelong friend Greil Marcus, the only other OG rock critic who’s kept doing it this long (or this well). In one of the most surprising moments, the legendary songwriter Randy Newman recalls their friendship, and admits he wrote a song about Christgau and Dibbell, “Lost Without You,” inspired by the closeness of their marriage. It’s the kind of movie where you come for the rock, stay for the romance.

Rolling Stone met up with the couple at the same East Village pad they’ve called home for 50 years. The place is packed with albums, books, art — the first thing that greets you at the door is a painting of the Shirelles. They talked about the doc, seeing their marriage up on the big screen, the art of arguing, playing hoops with Randy Newman, and the strange college semester when Christgau was Gene Simmons’ professor.

Congratulations on the movie.Robert Christgau: It came out really well. When [director] Matty [Wishlow] called me up and asked if I would do it, the first thing I said was, “Yes, if you include my marriage,” which at the time I think took him aback. However, he came to feel that it was the marriage that made the movie, which is what I believe.

It is the marriage that makes the movie.Carola Dibbell: But it’s still about you. I’m a co-star. Related Content Andrew Watt on His Insane 2026:  Madonna, McCartney, the Stones, Gaga  The Rolling Stones' Release Date for ‘Foreign Tongues’ Deluxe Edition Look for the Legends in the Best Rock Album Race at 2027 Grammys Alexander Skarsgård Embraces His Magnetism in the Rolling Stones’ Video for ‘Mr. Charm’

When I first saw it, I told the director, “This is a love story. A very strange love story.”Christgau: Well, I agree. I think that’s the best thing about the movie. The relationship really has a kind of vitality to it that you can see. And that’s exactly how I feel about Carola, and that’s the most important thing in my life. And it’s really nice that it actually comes through in the imagery of the film. I think that’s the reason people like the movie, too.

When did you two get together?Dibbell: The summer of 1972. Bob and I had known each other. He was my friend Dominique’s boyfriend. Bob had had his eye on me all this time, but I was just so delighted to have him as a friend. I knew that he was a rock critic, but I really was not like a groupie. I met him in the summer of 1970 — we were all having breakfast at Ratner’s Deli. But I then got into an argument with you about Godard.

Christgau: She knew more about film than I did.

Dibbell: Bob and I had a big argument about it, but then we became friends anyway, and then he began to date Dominique, and so we just knew each other. But eventually, everything changed for me.

Christgau: I’m so glad it did, Carola. She was an incredibly cute woman with a Radcliffe degree.

Dibbell: The thing is we were both English majors. One night we were playing a party game called “Celebrity,” and we needed to come up with a celebrity whose initials were an M and a C. And we both came up with Martin Chuzzlewit [the title character in an 1844 Dickens novel].

Now that’s two people destined to be together. I think that’s why people respond seeing such an unusual couple onscreen.Christgau: What makes it so unusual?

Two people, very extreme personalities, who stay madly in love for 50 years of marriage, but remain individuals in a totally unfiltered way.Christgau: I don’t know how extreme I think we are, but—

Dibbell: Really? I really don’t know that, but I believe you.

You both make a strong impression. Let me put it that way.Dibbell: Well, at the time that we got together, it was … I’m not going to say “turning point,” but it was sort of a point where one chapter in the counterculture and the movement was easing into another. People were asking, “Oh, is it OK to be a feminist and get married?” Bob was a feminist too, and he always liked smart women. And so we both were trying to figure out, how do you do this? A marriage of equals?

Something I love about the documentary is how it captures your enthusiasm for the art of a good argument. Dibbell: I used to say that if I told him “I agree with you,” he’d say, “That’s where you’re wrong.” He just couldn’t stop arguing.

Dibbell: Yeah, you. Who do you think we’re talking about? But it just comes very easily to both of us.

Would it be fair to say that you both have argumentative personalities?Christgau: I don’t think Carola has an argumentative personality.

Dibbell: There’s where I disagree with you.

I guess I mean a “debate” more than an “argument.”Dibbell: I think I argue more than I debate, actually. But it definitely improves our thought to be arguing together.

Christgau: I got Carola to start writing rock criticism, not because she was my wife and I wanted to give her the work — although, obviously, that was part of it. But because A, I knew she could really write, and B, she had knowledge of the subject.

Dibbell: I found rock criticism so interesting as a form, being a writer, and I was very interested in the unreliable narrator and all that kind of thing. Then when I read Lester Bangs, I said, “Oh, yeah! Why not be literally ambitious while writing about this declassé music stuff?”

Christgau: He could also write a paragraph in about a minute and a half.

When you began writing in the Sixties, there wasn’t a lot of serious attention paid to pop music.Christgau: But Rolling Stone was doing that a lot. Rolling Stone was a crucial part of why all of that happened. Jann Wenner had a head for finding the most interesting writers, many from the Boston college scene, and that was a really important factor in why I got to do what I did. No question about it.

And also the fact that I was already friends with Greil Marcus. That was a crucial part of it as well. He was at Rolling Stone, and frankly, I think he had Jann Wenner around his little finger. Because Jann was smart enough to know that this guy was really something else.

Early on, you wrote that your biggest influences were Thelonius Monk and Alan Freed.Christgau: Let me tell you, Monk has lasted. I still play a lot of Thelonious Monk. Carola gets a little tired of it.

Dibbell: I finally say, “Can we listen to The Clash?”

But you always had an appreciation for AM radio. You were open to tawdry pop trash.Christgau: It wasn’t “tawdry.” Come on.

You were writing in the Seventies about how great KC and the Sunshine Band were. In the Village Voice.Christgau: It’s all well-made, that’s the thing. Extremely well-made. That proves my point.Dibbell: It proves your point.

Determined as you are to undermine the entire premise of my point, I’m going to make it anyway. When I first read your Consumer Guide as a kid in the Eighties, I couldn’t believe there was an adult writing about Funkadelic and the Go-Go’s and Donna Summer and A Flock of Seagulls and taking it seriously, as art.

Christgau: Four hours a day listening to AM radio had something to do with that. But I wanted to write about pop art as an important phenomenon.

There’s a great story in your memoir about when you were teaching the rock criticism class at CUNY on Staten Island in 1970, and one of your students was a kid named Gene Klein.Christgau: Who later became Gene Simmons.

I always wonder what the dragon from Kiss learned from you about music critics.

Christgau: He just sat in the back and kept his mouth shut.

Something The Last Critic documents is your insanely obsessive online following, around the world.Christgau: One thing that happens with this movie is people in Sweden and Norway coming up with their dog-eared copies of my books.

Dibbell: It was so funny hearing about Europeans with tattered versions of the first Consumer Guide book.

Christgau: So I had this fanbase all over the world, and I had no idea it was there, really. I was writing for the Village Voice, and they paid me decently, and I had a lot of autonomy, and I really valued it.  But when that ended, I kept writing. I managed to have a whole life as a critic, and it’s not like I’m working for Variety or the Times. I feel not just fortunate, I feel like I built something.

Dibbell: But there was a point when you were having conversations about whether you should stick with the Consumer Guide or whether you should write more essays. Also, I remember I had to argue Bob into writing the memoir, Going Into the City. You felt, “Why would anybody want to read my story?”

Christgau: Which came out pretty well, I think.

Dibbell: Yeah, it did. But you resisted that. Editors thought you should write more essays, but I felt that the Consumer Guide was such a great form that you shouldn’t stop doing it. And I also understood that you had a fanbase based on that. I wasn’t even thinking so you can make a living — but just with me, my constant struggle to get a book published, I just felt this is a great thing, that fanbase. You’re very lucky that people want to be your fan.

How did you become friends with Randy Newman? He plays such a surprising role in the movie. Dibbell: He was lovely.

Randy Newman talks about writing a beautiful love song about you two, “Lost Without You.”Christgau: I will say I was very proud. I wrote about Randy in the very beginning, and I felt that Randy really did understand that I got him. I was early on it. I was initially assigned by this guy from BMI named Russ Sanchez when I was writing for the BMI magazine who told me about this songwriter guy named Randy Newman who they wanted to have a piece on. At that time he lived in a house somewhere in the Valley, so I went there and I interviewed him. And then we went out to the ballpark and played basketball. This was a long time ago — I don’t play basketball anymore. But we had a game of basketball.

Dibbell: Don’t you each remember that the other one won?

Christgau: Well, he was taller than me. But I do rebound with a certain amount of verve.

It started with basketball, but how did that turn into a long-running friendship?Dibbell: He wrote you a fan letter in the Nineties, saying that he admired your perseverance, the way you kept up with new music, that it was something he did not actually understand, your enthusiasm for it. But he was interested in hip-hop and he wanted you to guide him. He wanted you to recommend him some hip-hop.

What did you play him?Dibbell: Public Enemy, I think.

Christgau: I’ve always had a high opinion of him.

Dibbell: We had lunch with him — this was in the old days when we had an answering machine. We got a message from someone claiming to be Randy Newman, and I said, “Oh, it’s not Randy Newman.” But you got back to him and said, “Was that you?” And he said, “Yes.” You were both old by then.

Christgau: We went to lunch. Then he came back to our place, even though he could hardly walk.

Dibbell: He had some bad knee problem, but you wanted to play him some new music. He climbed the stairs. Then he looked around our apartment, and he said, “If you wanted to fix this place up, I could loan you some money.”

He’s so sincere in this movie — we’ve never seen this side of him before. It’s probably the only Randy Newman song anyone would want to be about them.Christgau: Yeah, it’s a great compliment. I liked that song before I knew it was about us.

Were you surprised by The Last Critic, when you finally saw it?Christgau: I think a better way of putting it is that I was more pleased by it than I anticipated being. And I was especially happy about how important a role Carola played in it. Matty hadn’t made a movie before. This was not his area of expertise. But he ended up making a really good movie.

It just seemed like, “OK, you want to do this? What do you see in a documentary about a critic?”

But it goes beyond that. It’s the love story, in a collaborative life of the mind.Christgau: That is the thing that I like best about it, and I’m proud of it. Obviously, I’m very happy who it was a love story with. If it had been about [the legendary New Yorker and Village Voice journalist] Ellen Willis [his Sixties ex] and me, it wouldn’t have been this good. Ellen’s as smart as anybody I’ve ever met. But Ellen didn’t like music as much as Carola ended up doing. [Dibbell comes in from the next room.] I was just saying you were a better rock critic than Ellen Willis.

Dibbell: I respect her tremendously. Her work was foundational.

You were on the scene for so many pivotal rock moments, like the Monterey Pop festival and Woodstock. A fan on your Substack recently found a photo of you in the crowd at Monterey. Christgau: About the third row, yeah. Nobody at that time understood how important Monterey was going to turn out to be historically, as this event that really just pretended something was happening — but then it really happened. Woodstock itself was a strange and interesting experience, which involved a lot of lying around the grass, among other things.

The way you wrote about women musicians in the 1970s was very ahead of the curve culturally. You were engaging with feminist ideas at a time when it was rare in music journalism. There’s a really moving moment in the doc when the writer Jessica Hopper discusses reading your words on Joni Mitchell.Christgau: Let it be said that Ellen Willis was not without her presence in that fact, because Ellen Willis really made me a much more fervent and conscience-driven and militant feminist. It was really important to me to be a feminist critic. I mean, I had those impulses anyway, but Willis obviously solidified them, without any question. I’ve been writing about women making rock & roll since the beginning. Joy of Cooking and Fanny are bands that 90 percent of people have never heard of.

You were taking Dolly Parton seriously as a writer in the 1970s, when most of the media treated her as a joke.Christgau: But Patti Smith was out there covering “Jolene,” right? Glad she’s still around. How old is Patti?

Dibbell: She’s a little younger than us, but not that much younger than us. So, what, she’s in her seventies?

She turns 80 in December.Dibbell: And Debbie Harry? I think she’s older than me.

You had a great line about a Billy Joel album in the Eighties: “Sexual-politics rads like me were fretting about a decade ago come home to haunt guys who thought they were a crock.”Christgau: I said that? That’s pretty good. But as far as my marriage with Carola is concerned, one thing that’s really significant about how it happened is that I went out with one of her best friends, for close to a year before. And so Carola was someone I really knew fairly well, but it wasn’t like we were dating.

Dibbell: Not even a little bit. I was really not ready to get married again in that time. I’d been married before — I got married on my way to get divorced. I was not ready for a potential husband, so I was very happy to know Bob as a friend.

As you said before, you were figuring out a new way of doing this — a marriage of equals. Dibbell: Well, I had to figure out how to be heard, when you were surrounded by people who were just going to listen to you. I had to figure out how to do that. Despite all the struggling to be an equal and all that, I do spend a lot of time feeling like Bob is doing what he’s doing, and I’m helping make it work. But at the same time, I mean, when I finally published a novel [The Other Ones, in 2014] and had readings and did events as myself, it was very different. And Bob was great. He came as my date on an event I did at Rochester [New York]. He said “I love being the date. I love not having to do the work.”

Some of the best moments in the doc are just you two geeking out about music together.Christgau: There was an emotional weight to it that most documentaries about critics wouldn’t have. I just understood that the marriage was integral to the fact that I did this work, and therefore it had to be there.

Dibbell: I believe Bob when he says that, but I don’t necessarily experience it that way. I mean, I rarely talk you out of an opinion about a record.

Dibbell: I mean, I really was amazed by how much of this movie was about work, judgment, criticism. So there are all these shots where he’s writing at his computer, with all these piles of books collapsing around him. And he’s sitting there thinking, “Is this an A or an A-minus?” But one of my favorite scenes is when I’m editing Bob. Just because it seemed so relaxed and there were so many things we agreed about without really having to spell them out. And I like that. I like that a lot.

I’m just so used to this setup — our marriage, how we interact with each other — I don’t even think about how it works. There’s just so much that we share. I’m so used to it. Christgau: After half a century, I would hope you’re used to it.

#3275. 10 Hacks Every Hulu User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you don't like the content Hulu is suggesting for you, you have several options to curate your recommendations. "Disliking" a show or movie removes it from your Home view and You May Also Like entirely, so the only way you'll see that content is if you search for it. You can dislike on the Details page if you're watching on your TV or use the thumbs down on mobile or web. (The "Like" button will obviously influence your algorithm in the opposite way). If your "Continue Watching" queue is cluttered with shows you started but didn't like enough to finish, you can remove them from your watch history as well as the My Stuff list. This, too, will allow content to remain searchable but not suggested in other areas of the app.

If PIN protection is enabled, users must enter a four-digit PIN when switching between profiles on a single account. This is intended as a parental control feature, since it's available on non-Kids profiles and can keep children from accessing more mature content on an adult's profile. However, you can also enable this feature to keep other users from seeing your viewing history and preferences or influencing your algorithm by watching their content under your profile (accidentally or on purpose). To set up a PIN, log into your account on Hulu's website, select your profile, and go to Manage Profiles > Parental Controls. You'll have to choose a PIN and enter your password to confirm the changes.

Another approach to protecting your profile and algorithm is to set up separate profiles for specific use cases, such as when you have guests or if you host watch parties for certain shows. This keeps content from influencing your recommendations and prevents other viewers from seeing what's in your watch history or saved content (especially if there are things you want to keep private).

If you find that subtitles and captions are too bold—or not visible enough—you can change the font, color, size, and style from the default so they enhance your viewing experience rather than detracting from it. Hulu allows you to adjust the color and opacity of the font, background, and window so you get the right contrast, and you can also select the specific font and font scaling. On your streaming device, go to Settings > Subtitles & Captions, then hit the back button on your remote to save your preferences. You can update these settings on mobile and desktop as well.

If you have a long list of shows and films to watch but can't decide what to start next, look for the "Expiring Soon" badge to see which titles are leaving the service in the next two weeks. Badges display the number of days remaining, so you can determine what to prioritize and whether it's worth diving in based on how much time you have to finish before the expiration date. Go to "My Stuff" to monitor saved titles that are expiring soon.

If you've been watching Hulu under an account shared with family or friends and need to switch to your own subscription, you can transfer your profile to keep your watch history and settings intact instead of starting from scratch. You can initiate a profile transfer on a TV-connected device. Note that account holders have to approve transfer requests within seven days, and once expired, transfer requests cannot be resubmitted—so be sure to let the primary user know that you've made the request.

If you've shared your Hulu login information with friends or activated your account on devices you don't own, you may want to regularly audit where your account is being used and remove any that don't need access. This includes TVs in Airbnbs and hotels. If you stay logged in, unauthorized users may have access to your Hulu account and personal data. You can see activated devices (and their activation date) under Your Account > Watch Hulu on Your Devices > Manage Devices. Click Remove next to old or unrecognized devices.

Hulu has an offline mode that allows you to download shows and movies to watch when you don't have a network connection. This is useful for traveling or when you know your wifi or cell service will be limited. Downloads are only available on supported iOS and Android devices, which means you may have to consider how much space your content takes up. You can select High for video quality if you want maximum resolution, but you may want to choose Standard if you are short on storage. This option is available under Downloads > Settings > Video Quality on iOS and Account > Settings > Downloads > Video Quality on Android. Note that once you click play on downloaded content, you have 48 hours to watch it before it expires—so don't start it unless you are ready.

If you have a Hulu + Live TV subscription, you must designate a "Home" network, which determines the local channels included in your plan. You can update your location up to four times within a 12-month period, but this limitation is meant to prevent viewers outside a household from sharing a subscription. Hulu does allow you to stream live TV on mobile when you're away from your home network (within the U.S.) as long as you access your account on that network every 30 days. If you travel often, check in with your mobile device frequently to avoid being locked out when you're away. Note that you can still watch streaming content with no restrictions.

#3273. New Apple TV comedy starring Elizabeth Banks, Ted Danson coming soon

Apple TV has announced a new comedy, She’s Fine, that’s coming soon with stars Elizabeth Banks and Ted Danson. Here are the details.

Earlier this year, Apple announced a high-profile new comedy in the works starring Elizabeth Banks, with later cast additions including Ted Danson and guest star Tom Selleck.

Now today that series, titled ‘She’s Fine,’ has gotten a release date and the first images have debuted.

She’s Fine premieres Wednesday, January 27 with two episodes, followed by weekly releases through March 24.

Fresh off a messy divorce, Heidi (Banks) sets out to secure a lively second act for herself and her kids. But when she stumbles into coordinating her father’s retirement community sexcapades, Heidi is forced into an unlikely alliance with his girlfriend’s perpetually single son.

Katey Sagal and Rob Delaney also star in the half-hour comedy, which hails from creators Liz Heldens and Matt Ward.

Other notable Apple TV comedies include the Owen Wilson-starring Stick, which just returned for season 2. And Bad Monkey from the co-creator of Ted Lasso and Shrinking is coming back soon too.

Are you interested in watching She’s Fine? Let us know in the comments.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month, or you can get it discounted through the Apple One bundle.

#3272. Johnny Depp Pic ‘Ebenezer’ Counts $19M U.S. Opening As Moviegoers Pinch Pennies – Sunday AM Box Office Update

SUNDAY AM: It was the best of times at the box office and it was the worst of times: Paramount’s Johnny Depp comeback movie, Ebenezer, opened to No. 1, but under the $20M where tracking had been spotting it, with $19M.

Know that this isn’t a Depp problem, as 50% of the audience came because they were fans of the 3x Oscar-nominated star. There was no rush-out factor here with Ebenezer, because… c’mon, it’s a 183 year-old story that everybody knows. Thirty-four percent of the audience came for the subject-matter plot, while 8% of ticket buyers said it was part of a franchise they loved. Also, we need to consider the fact that there’s a box office tsunami coming in with Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping next weekend, which could do $100M. Quite often, moviegoers ease their attendance the weekend before a big event film hits theaters.

Know the weekend result here isn’t a total bah-humbug for Ebenezer, as there’s still some Christmas wish left in the film: It has great audience exits with A- CinemaScore, 90% audience rating on Rotten Tomatoes, and 4.5 stars on Posttrack. There’s enough good will here for Depp’s Mr. Scrooge to find an audience over the Thanksgiving holiday and beyond, particularly among the older set, who we know is slow to come out and are returning during the 2026 box office boom. Watch on Deadline

Also for the pic’s net $38M production, this opening isn’t bad particularly given the fact that Christmas movies paynoff like Domaine de la Romanée-Conti wines in the long run for a major studio’s library. Depp took a $5M upfront fee, which is lower than his previous $20M average, as well as a back-end tied to the profit of the Emma Watts production.

Also realize that this movie in its old IP would have probably opened at this domestic level had it hit screens before the Depp-Amber Heard court trials. It’s not like this is a Johnny Depp non-franchise movie starring Timothée Chalamet and directed by Tim Burton.

Underscoring how older skewing this property is, the definite recommends on the Screen Engine/Rentrak PostTrak audience exits increased as each demo set got older from 10-12 year olds at 33% to 50% 18-24, 65% 25-34, 64% 35-44, 69% 45-54 to a huge high of 78% for the over 55 set. That tells you the type of picture Ebenezer is catering to with 54% over 35 and 34% over 45.

Saturday’s $7.1M off the pure Friday (sans previews) of $5.2M was +35%, which indicates there was some bump from families attending, which only repped 10% of the overall audience. Moms (essentially Depp fans) showed up at 65% with a 65% definite recommend, though Dads at 35% gave the Ti West-directed take of the Charles Dickens novella an 82% definite recommend. With genre fans not plentiful enough on this movie with 18-34 at 40%, the hope is that families might fill the void. The only thing here is that the nag factor from kids under 12 is low with 47% giving the PG-13 movie a must-see right away.

Gotta give credit to Paramount Global Marketing and Distribution boss Josh Goldstine for a creative, sticky and clever campaign here on Ebenezer. Word is, he pitched Depp on the idea of the actor getting into character as Scrooge for San Diego Comic-Con and other public appearances (the Jack Sparrow actor also went full method for a crowd in NYC). Again, the trailer drop for Ebenezer and Depp’s appearance in San Diego was one of Comic-Con’s bigger surprises.

RelishMix pointed out that word of mouth was positive on social for Ebenezer with a near 8 out of 10 buzz rating. “There’s a tone of relief, nostalgia and collective exhale that Depp is working again, with genuine curiosity about how he’ll stack up against Scrooge royalty like Alastair Sim, Albert Finney and George C. Scott. Fans are framing ‘this role less as a comeback and more as a victory lap after a rough few years.’ Fans exclaim, ‘Johnny Depp’s return is a reminder of why he’s regarded as one of the defining actors of his generation. Johnny Depp can simply play anything.'”

The social media reach across YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and X is 395M, 6% above other family-live action titles. Activation on Ebenezer runs at 50% with a total of 81.6M fans led by Johnny Depp at 56.7M fans, Rupert Grint at 5.51M and Charlie Murphy at 463K, while the other half of the cast is not-activated.

Overall weekend looks like an estimated $91.5M, +24% which is still higher than the same frame a year ago which was $74M.

1.) Ebenezer (Par) 3,535 theaters, Fri $6.7M, 3-day $19M/Wk 1

2.) The Cat in the Hat (WB) 4,003 theaters, Fri $2.5M Sat $5.4M Sun $3.5M 3-day $11.4M (-43%)/total $38.1M/Wk 2

How does a David Leitch directed action movie, even at this reported lower budget level of net $40M, lose a lotta cash? Amazon can’t always flip a movie to Prime after so-so testing. It always depends on the contract with the filmmaker. Women over 25 gave this movie its best definite recommend at 71%, but this film was for a Gen Z dude crowd and they only showed up at 21% behind older males (37%) and older females (28%). There was awareness but no interest among the Gen-Z crowd who looked at this dusty bank robbery concept as older filmmakers trying to preach hipness to them. The idea of robbers posting their robberies on YouTube is a very early aughts type of thing which Obsession generation doesn’t even buy. In fact, they don’t even go to banks: They’re too busy using Zelle. 8.) Wild Horse Nine (Sea) 2,175 (+1075) theaters, Fri $1.5M, Sat $1.8M Sun $1.3M 3-day $4.6M (-22%) /Total $13.3M/Wk 2

SATURDAY AM: Paramount is still looking at a $20M opening for the Johnny Depp comeback movie, Ebenezer, but rivals see it lower. The hope is that families show up today as we hear the Ti West genre fans didn’t come out in droves last night; Friday and previews at $6.7M. One indication that it’s appealing to families is that the AMC Disney Springs is the pic’s highest grossing location with close to $25K so far.

Other good news is that the movie is playing evenly throughout the country: East, South, Midwest, South Central, and Mountain. You never want a movie that just plays on the coasts. PLFs are accounting for 36% of the gross. CinemaScore is great A- with a 65% definite recommend which is alright on Screen Engine/Rentrak’s PostTrak, which could mean a slow burn. Diversity demos show 48% Caucasian, good 28% Latino and Hispanic turnout, with 12% Black and 6% Asian American. Big chuck is older skewing with 37% over 45 while the 18-34 set is 40%. Overall, the pic is leaning 52% female, with women over 25 the biggest demo at 41%, which is not surprising on a Depp movie.

Columbia Pictures and Mandalay’s action-thriller Ghost Soldier posted $1.55M on Friday from 2,558 locations for a $4.9M 3-day and $8M five-day. The core audience likes it at 90%, they just didn’t show up in droves. The pic at net $18M, co-financed by TSG is cheaper than Amazon MGM Studio’s How to Rob a Bank which cost $40M before P&A. Older audience here at 49% over 45 with 57% guys and 55% Caucasian, 22% Latino and Hispanic, 14% Black, and 4% Asian American. Pic is playing best in South and South Central where close to 40% of the gross is coming from versus a norm of 27% for other movies in the marketplace. The Harkins Estrella Falls 16 in Arizona is the leading single-location with $4K since Friday.

The David Leitch directed action movie How to Rob a Bank needs to rob more to pump up its gross after a $2.2M Friday/preview for what looks to be a $4.7M opening. CinemaScore is a B-, which is lower than Leitch’s last movie, The Fall Guy, which landed an A-. Male leaning at 57%, with the 18-34 demo at 66%. Men over 25 were the biggest at 37%, followed by women over 25 at 28% and then men under 25 at 21%. The movie needed more of the latter to show up to make this work. Caucasians are 42%, Latino and Hispanic at 26%, Black at 15%, and Asian American at 9%. PLFs repping around 27% of the weekend so far. AMC Waterfront 22 in Pennsylvania is the top grossing venue with $13K.

It’s a low weekend at the box office with around $80M for all movies, though interestingly enough, it’s +8% from a year ago when Lionsgate’s Now You See Me: Now You Don’t opened to $21M. It feels like this is the calm before next weekend’s storm, which will be Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping which many believe has a shot to open at $100M.

We’ll have more updates and the chart for you later this morning.
